content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a new transformer-based object detector called HeatDETR. As the name implies, the detection head and training mechanism borrows from DETR. However, unlike DETR, the body of the network is mostly transformer-based, with initial patch embeddings CNN-based (similar to LeViT). The paper emphasizes real-time inference speeds and experimentally tests runtime across both GPUs and CPUs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper presents new tweaks and ideas when constructing a CNN/ViT hybrid and a transformer-based object detector.
- It presents experimental results across different hardware, and improves over many DETR-based baselines.

Weaknesses:
- The paper seems overly selective in its comparison with prior art. There are many object detectors out there that receive higher AP on COCO and simultaneously runs much faster. Take YOLOv4 (Bochkovskiy et al.) as an example of something two years old. It already boasts 43.5% AP at 62 FPS using a Volta GPU. With that in mind, 44% at 25.2 FPS does not seem to push the state of the art. Looking at Table 9 in something newer like YOLOv7 (Wang et al.), we see 51.4% at 161 FPS. This may be too new and should be considered concurrent work. However, even with the much older YOLOv4 comparison, the results do not seem enough. I suggest including more prior art, even the ones that are non-transformers or operate at a smaller input resolution. They still solve the same task so it a valid and appropriate comparison in the table. Let the reader decide whether or not this work still constitutes and important contribution in the genre of DETR-based detectors, given the full context. I do think it falls a bit short though.
- Instead of presenting a few clear-cut ideas that improve results, the paper presents a highly engineered solution that only modestly improves the much more straightforward DETR. This is also presented in a way that leaves a lot of question marks (I will have examples under the Clarity section), so I think it's difficult for other research to build upon this work.
- The hardware-awareness seems overstated. Calling a NVIDIA GTX 1080 and Intel i7 CPUs "resource-constrained" also seems really strange, because those together make a pretty high-end power desktop. Figure 1 confusingly has FPGA and a mobile phone in the schematic, but these genuinely more resource-constrained platforms are never tested.
- The claim that it is the first real-time DETR seems questionable. Apple ships a DETR-based network (HyperDETR) that runs in 6 ms (on an iPhone, which is far less capable than a V100!) and has written a blog post about it.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
- The presentation of the paper could be greatly improved. There are many terms that are not explained to the reader, and overall this was a really difficult paper to get through.
  * For instance, in section 3 under "Congestion 2", it is not clear what skip-connections or branching is being addressed, because it is unclear what the paper uses a starting point. The first paragraph is then followed by "Thus, Identity I becomes a candidate in our search space." I do not understand what the identity is replacing, and I do not quite get the references to "search space".  The first time "two-phase search space" is mentioned, this is not explained.
- Naming each component of the network (HOD, SAM, SCM, TCM) actually makes it harder to read.
- Ambiguous/unclear word choices can make the paper harder to read, since the intention is not clear. Here are a few examples:
  * "prejudice running speed" -> hamper running speed
  * "having trivial accuracy drops" -> having modest (negligible?) accuracy drops
  * "detection prevision (sic) without sacrificing both the convergence and inference speed" -> "detection precision sacrificing neither convergence nor inference speed"
  * "is more potential" -> "has more potential"

Quality:
- Overall, I do think all the new types of components (SAM with the upsample, SCM with hyper-column-like extraction) are not presented with particularly deep insight, but feel more like random modifications that each squeeze out a bit of improvement. There is always a cost of increasing the complexity of a model, and this makes the model quite a bit more complex (than a straightforward ViT or CNN with similarly repeated blocks, for instance). However, the added complexity only leads to modest improvements in terms of AP and inference speed.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents a modest improvement in a particular vein of object detectors. However, for actual deployment on resource-constrained environment, there are many detectors that offers better performance at a cheaper price (although they are not mention). The improvements are also overly complex and the writing is obtuse making it hard to absorb these new ideas. For these reasons combined, I do not think the quality of this paper is particularly high and I worry it will have limited impact if presented at ICLR.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes HeatDETR, a DETR-based detection model targeting high-speed inference on multiple edge devices. It contains several techniques, including the semantic-augmented module (SAM), the task-couple module (TCM), and the scale-combined module (SCM). It also applied hardware-aware NAS to further optimize the models. Experiments are conducted on COCO.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Improving the inference efficiency of DETR is an essential step toward deploying DETR-based detection models on real-world applications. I have some concerns regarding the manuscript:
1. Lack of ablation study experiments. The proposed model contains many components, and it also utilizes hardware-aware NAS to improve the results further, while the baseline models do not. Without extensive ablation study experiments, it is unclear where the improvements come from and whether each of the components is necessary or not. 
2. Lack of comparison with previous methods. Regarding TCM, [1] also targets reducing contradictions between classification and regression tasks. It is unclear to me whether we need TCM. Or directly applying [1] is sufficient. 
3. According to Table 2, the proposed models' improvements over strong baselines are limited. The practical value of the proposed models seems to be limited. 


[1] Tood: Task-aligned one-stage object detection, ICCV 2021

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a hardware-oriented detection pipeline named HeatDETR, which achieves both higher accuracy and better training inference efficiency across multiple devices. The paper claims three major contributions: 

1.  A backbone design that focuses on capturing local and global information. To enhance the low-level semantics, a semantic-augmented module (SAM) is introduced in the backbone with the global modeling capabilities of self-attention. To handle the conflicting objectives of classification and regression, they also introduced a task-couple module (TCM). 

2.   A scale-combined module (SCM) is then utilized, through which the multi-level detection process is transformed into a single-level process.  

3.  HeatDETR exceeds many DETR-based methods by 0.3%∼6.2% AP with 5%∼68% speedup on high-end GPU while requiring  28%∼92% fewer training epochs.

4. HeatDETR can achieve real-time inference on extremely memory-constrained devices such as Dual-Core Intel Core i7 CPU.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
1. HeatDETR can achieve real-time inference on extremely memory-constrained devices such as Dual-Core Intel Core i7 CPU.
1. HeatDETR exceeds many DETR-based methods by 0.3%∼6.2% AP with 5%∼68% speedup on high-end GPU while requiring  28%∼92% fewer training


Weakness


1.  Limited novelty. The paper is an integration of many existing components with some minor modifications. 
2.  The paper writing needs to be improved. It is not easy to distinguish the novel contributions of the paper. 
3.   In Page 2 it is mentioned that  “In addition, these generated models can be trained from scratch directly with 14 times fewer epochs than DETR”. Does it mean that HeatDETR can be trained from scratch without ImageNet pre-trained backbone?  It is well known that DETR takes a longer time to converge, but recent approaches such as DN-deformable DETR and DINO can be trained much faster. So is it fair to still compare the performance with DETR?

4. Pages3-4 It Is claimed that “HeatDETR is the first work on transformer-based detectors to explore comparable performance and fast inference speed on the resource-limited hardware while maintaining efficiency training”.  Please justify this statement considering that we have existing frameworks such as Mobileformer that utilize mobile-friendly transformer backbone networks on the DETR framework. 

5.  On Page 5, the proposed method replaces  LN with BN to improve the model efficiency. But, it is well known that BN may cause the model performance to fluctuate with the batch size, and it may lead to inferior performance while using small batch sizes. 
6.  Table 2.  MobileFormer reports a higher accuracy of 43+ while being trained for 300 epochs but the authors report their 12 epoch results only.  It is not clear to me why MobileNet 300 epochs results are not reported while DETR 500 epoch results are included in the table.  
7.  Page 8 it is mentioned that: “the transformer-based methods generally outperform CNN-based Methods”. This does not seem to be true. Existing (published) SOTA methods such as DyHead and HTC ++ are still CNN-based. 
8.  Fig. 6. Mobileformer and similar transformer-based backbone methods reporting their object detection results on the DETR framework need to be included in this comparison.

Minor comments 

Page 3: “End-to-end detectors delete sophisticated post-processing like NMS”. Instead of “delete”  It will be better to mention that “ " End-to-end detectors do not require  sophisticated post-processing like NMS"
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The proposed framework is an integration of multiple diverse components and the framework has limited novelty. Clarity of the paper needs to be improved and novel contributions of the paper need to be better clarified.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper has some interesting results, but the proposed framework is slightly below the ICLR acceptance rate. Paper writing can be improved and some of the bold claims mentioned above  (weakness) can be removed.
